summary: Proposes an informal management model for Diffserv routers, defining datapath elements such as classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues and schedulers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This draws a picture of the parts inside a router that sorts and prioritizes traffic.

subtitle: A conceptual blueprint for managing traffic in Diffserv routers.

tldr.problem: Diffserv routers need complex configuration to treat different traffic streams with different service levels, but router implementations vary widely, making it hard to manage networks of mixed equipment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a conceptual model of a router's datapath using modular functional elements (classifiers to sort traffic, meters to check rates, actions to mark or drop, queues to schedule), showing how they interconnect to realize different per-hop behaviors.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators and configuration tools can use this abstract model to consistently configure and manage Diffserv routers from different vendors without understanding vendor-specific implementation details.

facts.label: Functional elements
facts.value: Classifier, Meter, Action, Queue, Scheduler, Algorithmic Dropper

today: RFC 3290 is an Informational RFC that serves as the conceptual foundation for Diffserv router management. It has informed the design of SNMP MIBs and policy management protocols for configuring Diffserv networks. Network operators and equipment vendors continue to use this model to build consistent management interfaces for router configuration and monitoring.

sections.title: Introduction to Diffserv Router Management
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) allows network operators to offer different service levels to different traffic streams. A router marks each packet with a Diffserv codepoint (DSCP) in its IP header, and core routers forward packets according to their per-hop behavior (PHB) indicated by the DSCP, without examining the packet in detail.

This approach scales well because many traffic streams can be aggregated into a small number of behavior aggregates (BAs), each forwarded using the same PHB, simplifying router processing. However, Diffserv networks need coordinated configuration and management tools to provision and monitor routers consistently.

This document does not specify how routers must be built internally. Instead, it proposes an abstract management model that abstracts away vendor-specific implementation details, showing the configuration parameters needed to support Diffserv functionality. Network administrators and management tools can use this model to configure routers from different vendors in a coordinated manner, as if all routers had the same internal structure.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC draws a picture of the insides of a Diffserv router so that people managing networks can configure them all the same way, even though different routers are built differently.

sections.title: The Router Datapath Model
sections.content:
The model shows a Diffserv router with three main components: a routing core that moves packets between interfaces, an ingress interface where packets enter, and an egress interface where they depart. The routing core is modeled as having infinite bandwidth and zero delay; any queuing delay or loss is modeled on the interfaces.

At both ingress and egress of each interface, the same set of functional datapath elements can be arranged: Classifiers sort incoming traffic into streams based on packet headers or attributes, Meters check whether traffic conforms to a rate profile, Actions apply treatment such as marking the packet with a DSCP or dropping it, and Queuing Elements store packets temporarily and schedule their departure.

These elements can be arranged in series and in parallel, forming a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that describes the traffic conditioning and queuing behavior each packet experiences. Edge routers (at the network boundary) implement more configuration complexity than core routers, applying initial marking and policing. Core routers simply forward according to the DSCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a packet enters a router at one door. It goes through a series of machines: one checks what kind of packet it is, another checks if it is sending traffic too fast, another might give it a special mark, and another queues it for the right door to exit from. This RFC shows how to describe all those machines and how they connect.

sections.title: Classifiers, Meters and Actions
sections.content:
Classifiers are 1:N devices that split a single incoming traffic stream into multiple outgoing streams. They use filters that match packet header contents (such as the DSCP, IP addresses, TCP ports) or implicit attributes (such as the incoming interface). A Behavior Aggregate (BA) classifier looks only at the DSCP; a Multi-Field (MF) classifier looks at multiple packet fields such as source address, destination address, protocol, and TCP or UDP ports. Filters can overlap, so precedence rules must be defined to resolve ambiguity.

Meters are 1:N devices that measure traffic rate against a temporal profile and route packets to different outputs based on conformance level. A meter might classify traffic as conforming, partially-conforming (yellow), or non-conforming (red). Meters use profiles such as simple average rate, exponential weighted moving average (EWMA), or token bucket, each with parameters like rate (in bits per second) and burst size.

Action Elements process packets based on classification or meter results. A DSCP Marker sets or re-marks the Diffserv codepoint. An Absolute Dropper discards packets unconditionally. A Counter increments statistics for billing or monitoring. A Multiplexor merges multiple traffic streams. These actions determine whether a packet is forwarded, marked, delayed, or dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Classifiers recognize traffic by looking at its address label, meters check if the traffic is going too fast, and actions then decide to either let it through, mark it, slow it down, or throw it away.

sections.title: Queuing: Queues, Schedulers and Droppers
sections.content:
Queuing elements modulate packet departure and determine packet ordering. FIFO Queues store packets in the order received. Queues have a current depth, which can be monitored, and one or more thresholds that trigger other actions. Size limits are modeled by placing an Algorithmic Dropper before a queue; the dropper selectively discards arriving packets based on queue depth or other algorithms such as Random Early Detection (RED).

Schedulers gate packet departure from one or more queue inputs based on a service discipline. A scheduler may use static parameters like relative priority of inputs, absolute rate limits for minimum or maximum rates, packet-length or DSCP values, and absolute time. Possible disciplines include first-come-first-served (FCFS), strict priority, weighted fair queuing (WFQ), and rate-based scheduling. Schedulers can be work-conserving, always forwarding packets when they are available, or non-work-conserving, intentionally delaying packets to enforce a rate profile (traffic shaping).

The RFC specifies a minimal set of scheduler parameters: a minimum service rate profile (for rate guarantees), a service priority (for allocating excess bandwidth), and a maximum service rate profile (for non-work-conserving shaping). This abstraction allows a broad variety of scheduler implementations to be managed consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Queues hold packets waiting to go out, schedulers pick which queue to send from next (maybe giving priority to some, or dividing fairly), and algorithmic droppers decide when to throw packets away if too many arrive.

sections.title: Traffic Conditioning Blocks and Configuration Hierarchy
sections.content:
Traffic Conditioning Blocks (TCBs) combine low-level functional elements into self-contained reusable modules. A TCB has one input and one or more outputs and encapsulates a set of traffic conditioning functions (classification, metering, marking, policing, queuing) needed to implement a network policy. TCBs can be instantiated at each interface's ingress or egress, in series and in parallel.

The model defines a three-level management hierarchy. At the lowest level are individual functional datapath elements with their own configuration parameters and counters. At the middle level are TCBs, one or more of which may be instantiated on each interface in each direction. At the top level are interfaces, each with ingress and egress functionality. Higher-level tools (outside the scope of this RFC) may further group interfaces into templates for repetitive configuration.

Examples of TCBs include a simple policer (meter plus dropper), a shaper (non-work-conserving scheduler that delays non-conforming traffic), a classifier with per-class queuing, and configurations supporting multiple customers or microflow-based services. The TCB abstraction enables configuration tools to work with router management interfaces (such as SNMP or COPS) consistently, translating abstract policy into device-specific configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than configure classifiers, meters, and queues one by one, administrators group them into reusable "blocks" that implement policies like "customers in tier A get priority" or "automatically slow down traffic exceeding 1 Mbps", then place these blocks on interfaces.
